newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan cautiously confident on economy's prospects.
newsitem.headline: Japan cautiously confident on economy's prospects.

text.p: Japanese officials said on Friday they are confident that tumbling shares and a declining yen will not undermine the economic recovery, but they also betrayed some nervousness about the continued markets sell-off.
In a quarterly report, the central bank stuck to its recent assessment that the economy is recovering gradually and private demand is becoming more firm.
"We do not see them (the weak yen and the stock price plunge) as stalling the economy," said Masayuki Matsushima, head of the Bank of Japan's research and statistics department.
But he quickly added: "Further weakness in the yen could push up prices of imports, and the bank needs to watch to see if this will have an impact on Japan's economy."
The report said the central bank will closely watch the effect of recent falls in Japanese stock prices on corporate business sentiment.
While government officials have been speaking confidently, they privately express concerns about the market falls and fear any wrong words will accelerate the declines.

Economists said the central bank would have to maintain Japan's interest rates at their current record low level at least until it is assured that the recent financial turmoil does not gravely affect the economy.
Many economists predict the easy monetary stance will continue at least until mid 1997.
Japan's interest rates have been at record low levels since September 1995, when the Bank of Japan (BOJ) cut its key lending rate to 0.5 percent.

"Having seen the decline in the stock market, they (the BOJ) are getting more nervous about things. We see the bank continuing to loosen its monetary policy rather than tightening it," said Jason James, a strategist at James Capel in Tokyo.
Japan's economy has been recovering slowly since the start of last year without any signs of inflation after emerging from four years of negligible growth.
Towards the end of last year, speculation grew that the Bank of Japan might tighten its credit grip amid a firm performance by the economy.
But pessimism has grown rapidly as the government has proposed a tight budget for the coming year and the Tokyo stock market and the yen have dropped sharply since late last year.

On Friday, the Tokyo market's key barometer, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares, fell 1.23 percent to close at 17,689.36. The dollar hit a fresh 47-month high, rising above 120 yen in late Tokyo trading.
Weak share prices make it harder for companies to raise capital, which can make them cautious about investment in plant and equipment -- a key engine of the nation's economy.
A weak yen against the dollar makes imports more expensive for Japan, pushing up overall prices.

Japan's recovery is widely expected to slow in the first half of 1997/98, beginning on April 1, due to a planned rise in the consumption tax from April, but it is expected to maintain growth of above one percent in the whole 1997/98 after estimated growth of 2.5 percent in 1996/97.
Meanwhile, a string of economic indicators announced on Friday showed mixed moves in the economy.

Japan's diffusion index of leading economic indicators, which predicts economic trends in the coming months, stood at 77.8 on a scale of 100 in November, staying above the so-called "boom or bust" mark of 50 for a third consecutive month.

Sales at department stores, a major indicator of private consumption, fell one percent in December from a year earlier to 1.13 trillion yen ($9.4 billion), marking the first year-on-year drop in five months.
Sales at chain stores in December fell 0.4 percent from a year earlier, but were up 36.8 percent from the previous month at 1.87 trillion yen ($15.5 billion). ($1=120 yen)
